en: The Great Amitābha Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One, Compiled and Edited by Wang Rixiu, Jinshi of the National Academy, Longshu. Part One:
The Assembly of the Dharma Gathering. Section One: The Assembly of the Dharma Gathering.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples. All were great sages who had attained mastery of supernormal powers.

Their names were: the Venerable Ajñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Sūryodgata, the Venerable Svāgata, the Venerable Mahācaṇḍa, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and the Venerable Ānanda—these were the foremost among them.
Furthermore, there were the assembly of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas:
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and all other bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa.
Furthermore, there were sixteen noble beings, including Bhadrapāla and others:

the Bodhisattva Susamīkṣita, the Bodhisattva Śraddhāmati, the Bodhisattva Śūnyatāgata, and the Bodhisattva Abhijñākusuma. All of them honored the virtue of the Great Being Samantabhadra, were endowed with the immeasurable practices and vows of all bodhisattvas, and dwelt securely in all dharmas of merit.
Such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these assembled together at one time. 2.
The Second Chapter: Ānanda’s Inquiry. At that time, the World-Honored One’s countenance was radiant and beautiful, surpassing that of other days.
Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Today the World-Honored One’s faculties are joyful and serene; your countenance is pure and radiant, exalted and magnificent, like a mirror that is bright, clear, and transparent both inside and out."
Since I have attended upon the Buddha, I have never beheld his majestic countenance as I do today.
Is this not because he is mindful of the Buddhas of the past, or of those of the present and future?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, Ānanda!”
"Did various devas instruct you to come and ask this question,
or did you ask it yourself? Ānanda replied:
"I have posed this question based on what I myself have seen.

The Buddha said, "That which you have asked surpasses the merit of making offerings to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas throughout a single world-system, as well as the merit of giving to all the devas and humans, down to the smallest crawling and flying insects; even if one were to continue for many kalpas, it would not approach even a hundred thousand million billionth part of this."
Why is this so? It is because all the celestial beings, kings, and commoners, down to the smallest of crawling and flying insects, shall all attain the path of liberation through your inquiry.

Ānanda! Just as there is the udumbara flower in the world, which exists in its fruit but its blossom is not seen, and only when a Buddha appears in the world does the flower appear—so too is a Buddha difficult to encounter, just like that flower.
"Now that I have appeared in the world, you have well understood my intention by posing this specific question; truly, you do not serve the Buddha in vain!
Listen attentively, and I shall explain it for you."
He replied: "I truly wish to hear it!
3. The Section on the Fifty-three Buddhas, Part Three. A Buddha said:
"In a past kalpa long gone, there were great multitudes beyond measure, boundless and inconceivable.
At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata; he taught and liberated immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the Way, and then entered parinirvāṇa."
Next there was a Buddha named Guangyuan (Far-Reaching Light); next a Buddha named Yueguang (Moonlight); next a Buddha named Zhantanxiang (Sandalwood Fragrance);
next a Buddha named Shanshanwang (Good Mountain King); next a Buddha named Xumitianguan (Sumeru Heavenly Crown);
next a Buddha named Xumidengyao (Equal Radiance of Sumeru); next a Buddha named Yuese (Moon Color); next a Buddha named Zheng (Correct).
Next, there was a Buddha named Vimala; next, a Buddha named Asaṅga; next, a Buddha named Nāgadeva;
next, a Buddha named Rātriprabhāsa; next, a Buddha named Sumeruśikhara; next, a Buddha named Acala-bhūmi;
next, a Buddha named Vaiḍūrya-sukusuma; next, a Buddha named Vaiḍūrya...
[There was a Buddha] of lapis lazuli-gold color; next there was a Buddha named Golden Treasury;
next a Buddha named Flame Light; next a Buddha named Flame Root; next a Buddha named Earth Seed;
next a Buddha named Moon Image; next a Buddha named Sun Sound; next a Buddha named Flower of Liberation; and next a Buddha named Adornment.
Prabhāsa; next there was a Buddha named Sāgarabodhivikrīḍita; next there was a Buddha named Jālinīprabha;
next there was a Buddha named Mahāgandha; next there was a Buddha named Virajovigata;
next there was a Buddha named Nirvidacitta; next there was a Buddha named Ratnārcis; next there was a Buddha named Citakūṭa; next there was a Buddha named...
After Śūrabala, there was a Buddha named Guṇadhara-mati; after him, a Buddha named Sūryacandraprabhābhibhū;
after him, a Buddha named Sūryacandravaiḍūryaprabha; after him, a Buddha named Anuttaravaiḍūryaprabha;
after him, a Buddha named Agryaśīrṣa; after him, a Buddha named Bodhikusuma; after him, a Buddha...
The Buddha named Candraprabha; next, a Buddha named Sūryaprabha; next, a Buddha named Puṣpavarṇarāja;
next, a Buddha named Jalamacandraprabha; next, a Buddha named Mohāndhakāravidhamana;
next, a Buddha named Vyūhātikrama; next, a Buddha named Śraddhāviśuddha; next, a Buddha named Supuṣya; next, a Buddha...
The Buddha named Majestic Power was followed by a Buddha named Dharma-Wisdom; next was a Buddha named Crane-Sound;
next was a Buddha named Lion-Sound; next was a Buddha named Dragon-Sound; and next was a Buddha named Abiding in the World—all such Buddhas have already passed away.
4. The Section on the Original Causes of Dharmākara. Fourth. The Buddha said:

"Next there was a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat; he was fully endowed with these ten titles and remained in the world teaching for forty-two kalpas."

At that time, there was a great king who, having heard the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, was filled with joy and attained awakening. He immediately renounced his royal throne to become a śramaṇa, known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara; he possessed such lofty talent and wisdom that none could equal his courage and vigor.
He went to where that Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and praised the Buddha in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s wondrous marks and form Are peerless throughout the world;
Far surpassing the sun, mani-jewels, Fire, the moon, and pure water.”
His majestic spiritual power is boundless, and his fame resounds through the ten directions;
all this arises from the power of samādhi, perfected through diligence and wisdom.
His upholding of awakening is like the vast ocean—profound, expansive, and without limit or bottom.
Ignorance, greed, and hatred have been dissolved without remainder;
having thus transcended the world, one’s admiration and reverence cannot cease.
As upright as the blossoms of a fine tree, there is no one who does not love and delight in them.
Wherever the people saw me, they were all filled with joy.
In generosity and pure precepts, in patience and diligence,
In meditative concentration and great wisdom— of these things, I vow to attain them.
May all who are in fear universally attain great peace;
may they transcend birth and death, and there be none who do not achieve liberation.
When I have attained Buddhahood, may I be like the Dharma King in every respect.

Even if one were to make offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would not equal the seeking of perfect enlightenment; through firm courage, one will surely achieve it.
This can cause immeasurable lands to be universally illuminated by light.
Saving and delivering more than the sands of the Ganges, whose majestic virtue can be measured?
My land and its adornments are uniquely sublime and exquisite.
For all who wish to seek rebirth there, it is pure, peaceful, and blissful.
May deliverance be eternal and boundless; may the Buddha graciously serve as my witness.
Having made such vows, I shall practice with diligence and never grow weary;
though I dwell amidst bitter suffering, I shall endure it and never regret it.
5. The Section on the Questions Regarding the Great Vows. Fifth. The Buddha said:
"At that time, after the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these verses, he again addressed the World-Honored King of Splendor Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!'"
I have resolved to attain unexcelled bodhicitta, vowing that when I become a Buddha, I shall be the most eminent among the countless Buddhas of the ten directions;
my wisdom shall be courageous and fierce, and the radiance from the crown of my head shall illuminate the ten directions without end.
The land where I dwell is spontaneously composed of the seven treasures, exceedingly bright, beautiful, and gentle.
My name and my title for transforming and delivering beings are heard throughout the countless worlds of the ten directions; there is no one who does not hear or know of them.

The countless devas and humans, down to the smallest crawling and wriggling insects, who are born in my land are all bodhisattvas and śrāvakas; their number is inexhaustible, surpassing all other Buddha-worlds.
"Is it possible for one such as this to attain it?
At that time, the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, knowing that his wisdom and insight were lofty and clear, and his aspirations were vast and great,
spoke to him, saying:
"It is like the great ocean: even if a single person were to measure it with a peck-measure without ceasing for kalpas, its bottom could still be seen;
how much more so for one who seeks the Way with a sincere heart and practices with unflagging diligence—what could such a person not attain?"
"What vow of yours has not been fulfilled?
At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara was filled with great joy upon hearing what the Buddha had said.

The Buddha then selected from among two hundred and ten million Buddha-fields all the good and evil of the devas and humans, as well as the coarseness and excellence of their lands, causing them all to appear in accordance with his heart's vows.
Dharmākara then unified his mind and subsequently attained the divine eye, through which there was nothing he did not see clearly.
Section Six: The Forty-Eight Vows The Buddha said:
"At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara went to a secluded place; his mind was tranquil and free from all attachments as he sat in silence in contemplation."
Having embraced the pure practices of that buddha-field and cultivated them accordingly,
he again approached the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I have already encompassed two hundred and ten million buddha-fields; therefore, I shall set forth the pure practices for adorning those lands.
I pray that you will grant me leave to speak, and that the Buddha will deign to listen and examine my words!
That Buddha said to him:
"Excellent! You may speak in full."
"When the assembly of Bodhisattvas hears of your vows, they will be inspired by them as a means of self-exhortation, and they too shall be able to cultivate the adornments of the Buddha-fields.
Dharmākara replied, "My first vow is:
when I become a Buddha, within my land there shall be no hells, hungry ghosts, birds, or beasts, nor even any kind of crawling or flying insects."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The second vow: when I become a Buddha, there shall be no women in my land;

all the devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects from countless worlds who come to be born in my land shall all be born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds made of the seven treasures.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The third vow: When I become a Buddha, whenever those in my land wish to eat, food of a hundred flavors shall manifest before them from bowls made of the seven precious gems; once they have eaten, the vessels shall naturally vanish."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The fourth vow: when I become a Buddha, the clothing desired by the people in my land shall arrive immediately upon thought; they shall have no need for cutting, sewing, pounding, dyeing, or washing."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The fifth vow: When I become a Buddha, throughout my land, from the ground up to the void of space, there shall be dwellings, palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, streams, and flowering trees—all composed of countless varieties of miscellaneous jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense. They shall be exquisitely adorned, wondrous and surpassingly sublime; their fragrance shall pervade the worlds of the ten directions, and all sentient beings who smell this fragrance shall cultivate the practices of a Buddha."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The sixth vow: When I become a Buddha, the people in my land shall all love and respect one another in their hearts, and none shall harbor mutual hatred or envy."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The seventh vow: when I become a Buddha, all those in my land shall be entirely free from the minds of lust, anger, and delusion."
"If I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The eighth vow: when I become a Buddha, the people in my land shall all possess a single virtuous mind, free from delusive thoughts; whatever they wish to say, they shall already know each other's intentions in advance."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The ninth vow: When I become a Buddha, those in my land shall not even hear the name of anything unwholesome, much less encounter its reality.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The tenth vow: when I become a Buddha, the people in my land shall know that the body is like an illusion and have no mind of greedy attachment.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The eleventh vow: When I become a Buddha, although there will be distinctions between the devas and the people of the world within my land, their physical forms shall all be of one kind—golden in color; their faces and features shall be upright, pure, and beautiful, with no further instances of ugliness or deformity."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The twelfth vow: When I become a Buddha, suppose that all the devas and humans in the countless worlds of the ten directions, down to the smallest crawling insects, were all to become human beings, and all were to become pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas; and suppose they were all to sit in single-minded meditation together to calculate my lifespan for thousands of billions of kalpas—there would be none who could know it.'"
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The thirteenth vow: When I become a Buddha, suppose that throughout each of the ten directions, across thousands of billions of worlds, there are devas and humans, down to the smallest crawling insects; if they were all to become human beings, and all were to become pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, and all were to sit in meditation with single-minded concentration, and together attempted to calculate the number of people within my buddha-field—whether it be several thousand, ten thousand, or millions—there would be none who could know it.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The fourteenth vow: When I become a Buddha, the lifespans of those in my land shall all be immeasurable kalpas, such that no one is able to calculate or know their number."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The fifteenth vow: When I become a Buddha, the happiness experienced by the people in my land shall be exactly like that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The sixteenth vow: When I become a Buddha, those in my land shall abide in the stage of right faith, free from inverted perceptions and far removed from conceptual discrimination; their faculties shall be tranquil, and wherever they dwell, they shall all attain parinirvāṇa."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The seventeenth vow: When I become a Buddha, my preaching of the sutras and practice of the Way shall be ten times greater than that of all other Buddhas."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The eighteenth vow: When I become a Buddha, all those in my land shall fully comprehend their past lives, knowing the events of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The nineteenth vow: When I become a Buddha, all people in my land shall attain the divine eye and see hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The twentieth vow: When I become a Buddha, all people in my land shall attain the divine ear, hearing the Dharma preached by hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, and shall be able to receive and uphold it all.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The twenty-first vow: When I become a Buddha, the people in my land shall attain the knowledge of others' minds, knowing the thoughts of sentient beings across hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The twenty-second vow: When I become a Buddha, all people in my land shall attain supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), such that in a single thought-moment they can traverse hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of worlds."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The twenty-third vow: When I become a Buddha, my name shall be heard throughout the countless worlds of the ten directions. May all Buddhas, each within their great assemblies, proclaim my merits and the excellence of my land.
May all devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling and flying insects, upon hearing my name, feel compassion and joy; may they all be reborn in my land."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The twenty-fourth vow: When I become a Buddha, the light from the crown of my head shall be exquisite and surpass the brilliance of the sun and moon by hundreds of thousands of billions of times."
"If I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The twenty-fifth vow: When I become a Buddha, my radiance shall illuminate countless worlds beneath heaven; all dark and obscure places shall become brilliantly bright. May all the devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling and flying insects, upon seeing my radiance, give rise to a heart of compassion and perform good deeds, and may they all be reborn in my land."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The twenty-sixth vow: When I become a Buddha, may all the devas and humans in the countless worlds of the ten directions, down to the smallest crawling and flying insects, who are touched by my radiance, have their bodies and minds become compassionate and harmonious, surpassing those of all other devas and humans.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The twenty-seventh vow: When I become a Buddha, if there are gods and humans in the countless worlds of the ten directions who have resolved their minds on Bodhi, uphold the fasts and precepts, practice the six pāramitās, cultivate various merits, and with a sincere heart make a vow desiring to be born in my land—when their lives are about to end, I, together with a great assembly, will manifest before that person and lead them to their next life, becoming a Bodhisattva of the stage of non-retrogression.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The twenty-eighth vow: When I become a Buddha, may all the devas and humans in the countless worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, hang silk banners, provide food for śramaṇas, erect stupas and temples, maintain pure precepts and fasts, perform various acts of merit, and single-mindedly fix their thoughts upon me—even if they do so for no more than a single day and night without interruption—shall certainly be reborn in my land.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The twenty-ninth vow: When I become a Buddha, if the gods and people of the countless worlds in the ten directions, with sincere hearts, believe in and rejoice in being born in my land, and recite my name ten times, they shall surely succeed in being reborn there;
except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the True Dharma.'"
"If I do not obtain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The thirtieth vow: When I become a Buddha, may all the devas and humans in the countless worlds of the ten directions, down to the smallest crawling insects, who have committed evil in previous lives, immediately repent and perform good deeds upon hearing my name, uphold the sutras and precepts, and aspire to be born in my land. At the end of their lives, may they all bypass the three evil paths and be reborn here, so that everything they desire is fulfilled according to their wishes."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The thirty-first vow: When I become a Buddha, may all the devas and people of the countless worlds in the ten directions, upon hearing my name, prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and pay homage with their heads bowed; may they rejoice, believe, and delight in practicing the bodhisattva path, such that no deva or human being fails to pay them respect."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The thirty-second vow: When I become a Buddha, if there are women in the countless worlds of the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, rejoice, believe, and find joy in it, and who resolve their minds on Bodhi and loathe their female bodies, then at the end of their lives, their bodies shall no longer be female."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The thirty-third vow: When I become a Buddha, all who are born in my land shall attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime to succeed me on the throne, with the sole exception of those who, by their original vow, desire to go to other realms to transform sentient beings, cultivate the bodhisattva path, and make offerings to various Buddhas; they shall be born there at will.

By the power of my majestic spiritual authority, I shall cause them to teach and transform all sentient beings so that they all give rise to faith, and cultivate the practices of Bodhi, Samantabhadra, Nirvana, pure Brahma-conduct, the most supreme conduct, and all virtuous deeds."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The thirty-fourth vow: When I become a Buddha, those in my land who wish to be born in other directions shall, according to their wishes, never again fall into the three evil realms."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The thirty-fifth vow: When I become a Buddha, may the Bodhisattvas within my land, desiring to go to immeasurable worlds to make offerings to the Buddhas with various requisites such as incense, flowers, banners, canopies, pearls, and necklaces, be able to reach them all in the time it takes to eat a single meal.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The thirty-sixth vow: When I become a Buddha, if the bodhisattvas within my land desire any of the ten thousand kinds of objects to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the ten directions, they shall have them appear before them at will;
once their offerings are complete, they shall return to my land before noon on that very day."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The thirty-seventh vow: When I become a Buddha, may the bodhisattvas within my land who uphold the sutras and dharmas, recite them, and proclaim them, necessarily attain eloquence and wisdom."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The thirty-eighth vow: When I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas within my land will be able to expound all dharmas, and their wisdom and eloquence shall be immeasurable."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The thirty-ninth vow: When I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas within my land shall possess the strength of a Vajra-Nārāyaṇa; their bodies shall all be the color of purple-gold, and they shall be endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. In preaching the sutras and practicing the Way, they shall be no different from all other Buddhas."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The fortieth vow: When I become a Buddha, the land shall be pure and clearly illuminate immeasurable worlds in the ten directions;
if Bodhisattvas wish to see all the adorned and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions within the jeweled trees, they shall appear instantly, just as one beholds one's own face in a clear mirror.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The forty-first vow: When I become a Buddha, even those Bodhisattvas within my land who possess few merits shall be able to see and know that the tree of my place of enlightenment is four thousand yojanas high."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The forty-second vow: When I become a Buddha, all the devas, humans, and all myriad things within my land shall be adorned, pure, radiant, and beautiful, with forms and colors so exceptionally distinguished that they are subtle to the extreme and beyond measure. Although sentient beings possess the divine eye, they will be unable to discern their names or numbers."
"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.
"The forty-third vow: When I become a Buddha, the people in my land shall, according to their aspirations, naturally hear whatever Dharma they wish to hear."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

"The forty-fourth vow: When I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas within my land shall all achieve spiritual perfection through wisdom; their crowns shall all emit radiance, and their voices shall be grand and resonant, such that their preaching of sutras and practice of the Path shall be no different from those of the Buddhas."
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The forty-fifth vow: When I become a Buddha, may all bodhisattvas in other worlds who hear my name, take refuge in me, and practice with diligence, all attain the samādhi of pure liberation;
and while abiding in this samādhi for even a single moment of thought, they shall make offerings to inconceivable numbers of Buddhas without losing their concentration.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.
'The forty-sixth vow: When I become a Buddha, may all bodhisattvas in other worlds who hear my name, take refuge in me, and practice with diligence, all attain the Samādhi of Universal Equality;
and until they achieve Buddhahood, may they constantly see immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas of all realms.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The forty-seventh vow: When I become a Buddha, may all bodhisattvas in other worlds who hear my name, take refuge in me, and practice with diligence, immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression.'"
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.

'The forty-eighth vow: When I become a Buddha, may the bodhisattvas of other worlds who hear my name, take refuge in me, and exert themselves with diligence, immediately attain the first patience, the second patience, and the third dharma-patience, and never regress from the teachings of all Buddhas.'"

"If I do not attain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha. Chapter Seven: The Verses Spoken After the Vows The Buddha said: "At that time, after the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these vows, he further spoke in verse: [Verse 1] My mind is firm and unshakable; I have brought forth the supreme resolve. If my vows are not fulfilled, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 2] I wish to adorn the Buddha-lands; I seek to purify them all. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 3] I wish to save all sentient beings; I seek to bring them to liberation. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 4] I wish to see the Buddhas of the ten directions; I seek to hear their sublime teachings. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 5] I wish to practice the path of the Bodhisattvas; I seek to perfect all virtues. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 6] I wish to transcend birth and death; I seek to reach the shore of Nirvana. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 7] I wish to manifest the light of wisdom; I seek to illuminate the world. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 8] I wish to turn the wheel of the Dharma; I seek to guide all beings. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 9] I wish to dwell in the realm of the Tathāgata; I seek to abide in eternal peace. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 10] I wish to realize the ultimate truth; I seek to benefit all who live. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 11] I wish to be honored by gods and men; I seek to be a refuge for all. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. [Verse 12] I wish to transcend all worlds; I seek to dwell in the land of bliss. If I do not fulfill these vows, I shall never attain Buddhahood. The Buddha said: "After the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these verses, he further made these vows: [The following verses continue the specific details of the forty-eight vows.]
"I now, before the Buddha, Make this special vow of sincerity:
May I obtain a body of the Ten Powers, With majesty and virtue unsurpassed."
Furthermore, he becomes a great king, wealthy and sovereign;
constantly bestowing all manner of treasures, he brings benefit and joy to the poor and suffering,
ensuring that all sentient beings shall forever be free from sorrow and affliction throughout the long night.
Generating all roots of goodness, I nurture the fruit of Bodhi.
When I attain Buddhahood, My fame shall transcend the ten directions;
Gods and humans will joyfully hear my name, And all shall come to be born in my land.
With the light of my wisdom, I extensively illuminate boundless realms;
I eliminate the darkness of greed, hatred, and afflictions within all sentient beings.
Those from the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animal realm shall also be born within my land;
all who come to be born there shall cultivate pure conduct.
Like the Buddha’s golden-hued body, their sublime marks will all be perfectly complete.
With a heart of great compassion, I shall universally rescue all who are drowning.
In future ages, I shall become a Teacher of Gods and Humans,
and within billions of worlds, I shall roar the lion’s roar of the Dharma.
All who hear this sound attain understanding, becoming further perfected and luminous.
Just as the Buddhas of the past engaged in acts of compassion, delivering countless and boundless sentient beings; so too shall it be.
My practice shall likewise be thus, so that all may ascend to the shore of enlightenment.
If this vow bears fruit, the great trichiliocosm shall tremble;
the celestial deities of the void will surely rain down rare and wondrous flowers.
8. Section on the Initial Cultivation of Wholesome Deeds. The Eighth. The Buddha said:
"At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, in the presence of that Buddha, amidst the great assembly of devas, māras, brahmās, nāgas, spirits, and the eight classes of beings, made these great vows."
At that moment, the earth shook violently, and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers which fell upon him.
From the air, a voice proclaimed:
"He shall certainly attain Buddhahood."
Thereupon, Dharmākara dwelt in true wisdom and, with courageous diligence, cultivated immeasurable merits to adorn his land.

For this reason, he entered samādhi and, throughout great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, practiced the bodhisattva path, giving rise to no thoughts of desire, hatred, or delusion; he gave rise to no perceptions of desire, hatred, or delusion; he was not attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or any phenomena; and through the perfection of the power of patience, he disregarded all sufferings.

They take sole delight in recollecting the roots of goodness cultivated by the Buddhas of the past; they practice the conduct of tranquility, remain far removed from falsehood, and steadfastly maintain sincerity and rectitude.

They constantly benefit sentient beings with a harmonious countenance and loving speech, and with faith, reverence, and respect for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they plant the foundations of all virtues by relying on the gateway of ultimate truth.

He well guards his verbal karma by not disparaging the faults of others; he well guards his bodily karma by not losing his moral discipline (*śīla*); he well guards his mental karma so that it is pure and undefiled.
He constantly benefits and brings joy to sentient beings through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
he causes all sentient beings to achieve merit and virtue, remaining far removed from coarse speech, thereby avoiding harming himself or others, and avoiding harming both self and other.
Cultivating virtuous speech for the benefit of oneself and others, one brings about the mutual benefit of both self and others.

Furthermore, by teaching and transforming sentient beings to practice the six perfections, one attains mastery over all phenomena, thoroughly comprehending emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the unconditioned, non-arising, and non-ceasing, thereby becoming fully endowed with the model of conduct and perfecting all roots of goodness.
Wherever they are born, according to their wishes, immeasurable treasuries of jewels spontaneously appear.
By bestowing these upon sentient beings to bring them joy, they carry out their work of teaching and transforming others.
He caused immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta; such virtuous deeds were so immeasurable and boundless that they could not be fully described.
Chapter Nine: Approaching the Buddhas. The Buddha said:
“When the Bhikṣu Dharmākara was practicing the bodhisattva path, he respected, honored, served, and made offerings to the various Buddhas without ever ceasing.”
As the Great Kings of the Four Quarters, they went to the Buddha’s dwelling, where they paid homage, prostrated, served, and made offerings.
As the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling, where he paid homage, prostrated, served, and made offerings.

Acting as the king of the Yāma Heaven, the king of the Tuṣita Heaven, the king of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and even as the Great Brahmā King, they went to the Buddha’s dwelling to pay respect, prostrate, serve, and make offerings.

Subsequently, while residing in Jambudvīpa, having received the consecration as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), together with his ministers, officials, and clansmen, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling to pay respect, prostrate, serve, and make offerings.
For the sake of the kṣatriyas, brahmins, and others, they went to the abodes of the Buddhas to pay respect, prostrate, serve, and make offerings.

In this manner, for immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, they drew near to various Buddhas and planted the roots of all virtues, thereby fulfilling their aspirations.
10. Chapter on the Fulfillment of the Vow to Become a Buddha. Chapter Ten: The Fulfillment of the Vow to Become a Buddha. The Buddha said:
"When the Bhikṣu Dharmākara was practicing the bodhisattva path, his physical form was upright and majestic, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics."

From his mouth there constantly issued the fragrance of sandalwood, and from all the pores of his body issued the fragrance of the utpala lotus; this fragrance universally perfumed immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable *nayuta* yojanas.
All sentient beings who smelled this fragrance gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, from his hands there constantly issued forth all kinds of clothing, all kinds of food and drink, all banners, flags, and precious parasols, as well as all music and every most excellent requisite, thereby benefiting and gladdening all sentient beings and causing them to return to the Buddha-way.

Thus, by accumulating merit and virtue for immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, his merit becomes perfected and his majestic spiritual power blazes forth; only then does he fulfill his vow and enter the rank of a Buddha.
11. The Eleventh Section on the Crossing Over of Crawling Creatures. Ānanda addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"Has the Bhikṣu Dharmākara already attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa?"
"Has he not yet attained Buddhahood,
or is he present now?
The Buddha said:

"That Buddha-Tathāgata comes from nowhere when he comes, and goes nowhere when he departs; he is without birth or extinction, and belongs neither to the past, the present, nor the future. Yet, solely to fulfill his vows and deliver all sentient beings, he currently resides in the West, a million worlds away from here.
That world is named Sukhāvatī; that Buddha is titled Amitābha, and it has been ten kalpas since he attained Buddhahood."

Furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he transforms and teaches countless devas and humans, even down to the class of wriggling and crawling insects, such that there are none who do not attain transcendence and liberation.
12. The Section on the Supreme Radiance of Solitude. The Buddha said:
"The radiance of Amitābha Buddha is most far-reaching and prominent; the radiances of all other Buddhas cannot compare to it."

Among the countless Buddhas of the ten directions, the light from the crowns of their heads illuminates one *li*, some illuminate two *li*, and some illuminate three *li*; thus extending further and further, there are those that reach as far as twelve million *li*.

Furthermore, there were those whose light from the crown of the Buddha’s head illuminated one world, some illuminated two worlds, and some illuminated three worlds; thus proceeding further and further, there were even those who reached as far as illuminating two million worlds.
Only the light from within the crown of Amitābha Buddha’s head illuminates thousands of millions of worlds without end or limit.
Why is it that the light of other Buddhas has varying degrees of distance? For what reason is this so?

When they were first Bodhisattvas, their vows and merits each had their own degree of magnitude; when the time came for them to become Buddhas, each attained according to what they had acquired, and for this reason, their radiance also differs accordingly.
If one acts with sovereign spiritual power according to one’s will, there is no difference provided that one does not need to rely on prior calculation.
Because Amitābha Buddha’s power of vows is boundless and his merit is transcendent, his radiance is exceptionally superior compared to that of other Buddhas.
13. Section on the Names of the Thirteen Buddhas, Part Thirteen. The Buddha said:

"The radiance of Amitābha Buddha is brilliant, exquisite, swift, and utterly peerless, being infinitely superior to the light of the sun and moon by thousands of myriads of koṭis. As he is the sovereign king of the radiances of all Buddhas, he is titled the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (Amitāyus).

He is also titled the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Unrivaled Light, the Buddha of Flaming King Light, the Buddha of Pure Light, the Buddha of Joyful Light, the Buddha of Wisdom Light, the Buddha of Uninterrupted Light, the Buddha of Inconceivable Light, the Buddha of Ineffable Light, and the Buddha who Surpasses the Sun and Moon."
The radiance of this light shines upon countless worlds, such that even the most obscure and dark places are perpetually and brilliantly illuminated.
Among the devas, humans, birds, beasts, and all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures, there is none who, upon seeing this light, does not rejoice and give rise to a heart of loving-kindness.
Those who were lustful, wrathful, or deluded, upon seeing this radiance, all turned toward goodness.

Those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—places of interrogation, scourging, and suffering—saw this radiance and were no longer afflicted by pain; after their lives ended, they all attained liberation.
Not only do I now praise the radiance of Amitābha Buddha; likewise, the countless Buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas throughout the ten directions all praise it in this same way.

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing of the majestic power and meritorious virtues of this light, take refuge in it day and night and praise it without ceasing, they will surely be born in that land according to their aspirations.
Furthermore, he shall likewise be praised by all bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

Although I have described the majesty, spiritual power, loftiness, and exquisite wonder of Amitābha Buddha’s radiance for a full day and night—even for an entire kalpa—it would not yet be exhausted; what I have said to you now is but a brief summary.

14. The Section on King Ajātaśatru, Number Fourteen. At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru, together with five hundred sons of elders, each holding a golden flower-canopy, came forward to offer them to the Buddha. They then withdrew to sit to one side and, hearing the exposition of the merits and radiance of Amitābha Buddha, were all filled with great joy.
Their hearts made this vow:
"When we later become Buddhas, may we all be just like Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing this immediately, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Prince Ajātaśatru and five hundred sons of elders shall, after incalculable kalpas, all become Buddhas, just like Amitābha Buddha."
Having practiced the bodhisattva path for incalculable eons, they have each made offerings to four hundred billion buddhas, and now they again make offerings to me.
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were all constantly my disciples; now, having arrived here once more, they have met with me again.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, there was none among them who did not rejoice, pay homage, and offer praise.
Chapter Fifteen: The Level Ground and Harmonious Atmosphere. The Buddha said:

"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, everything is composed of the seven natural treasures—namely, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and mother-of-pearl. Their substance is gentle and supple, and the ground is formed by the intermingling of these seven treasures."
Alternatively, the ground may consist entirely of a single jewel, its radiant color shining with wondrous purity, surpassing all worlds throughout the ten directions.
That land is vast and expansive beyond measure; the ground is everywhere level and even, without Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, or any other mountains;
nor are there great oceans, small seas, pits, hollows, wells, or valleys, nor is there any place of darkness.
There are no hells, hungry ghosts, sentient beings, or birds and insects, nor even the class of wriggling and crawling creatures;
there are no asuras, nor any dragons or spirits.
There is neither rain nor dew, only natural flowing springs;
there is neither cold nor heat, and the climate is perpetually spring-like, fresh, clear, and bright, beyond full description.
There are ten thousand kinds of spontaneous objects, such as food and drink of a hundred flavors; whatever the mind desires appears before it.
If the mind does not wish to use them, they vanish spontaneously, and according to what one thinks of, there is nothing that cannot be obtained.
In this Sahā world, there is the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), wherein all that is required by its devas manifests spontaneously;
yet compared to the spontaneous objects within this Buddha-field, those [of the heaven] fall short by ten trillionfold and cannot equal them.
16. The Division on Lecture Halls and Residences. Chapter Sixteen. The Buddha said:
"The lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha are all spontaneously formed from the alternating intermingling of the seven treasures."
Furthermore, there were pavilions and railings made of the seven treasures;
moreover, garlands of the seven treasures were suspended as ornaments along their sides.

Additionally, white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and maṇi jewels were interlaced to cover them entirely above, so exceptionally wonderful, exquisite, pure, and radiant that they cannot be fully described.
The palaces and dwellings inhabited by the other bodhisattvas and śrāvakas are likewise so.
For those devas and worldlings, clothing, food and drink, flowers, incense, necklaces, parasols, banners and pennants, and exquisite music appear at will according to their desires.

The palaces and towers where they dwell correspond in color, form, height, and size; they are all manifested through transformation, composed of either a single jewel, two jewels, or even immeasurable varieties of precious gems.
However, among the palaces and mansions, some may be as tall and vast as one desires, floating in mid-air like clouds;
others cannot be made as tall or vast as desired, remaining upon the ground like those of the mundane world.

The reason for this is none other than that those who can act according to their will did so because, in previous lives when seeking the Way, they practiced compassion and diligence, further cultivating various virtues until they became profound.

The inability to act according to one's will is caused by the fact that in previous lives, while seeking the Way, one did not cultivate diligence with a compassionate heart; it results from performing meager acts of goodness and possessing thin merit.
As for clothing and food, these are all equal, but only the palaces and dwellings differ.
Thus, there are distinctions between progress, diligence, and indolence, as well as differences in the magnitude of merit; these are shown for all to see.

This lecture hall and its palatial buildings were originally without a creator and have no point of origin; they have been produced through spontaneous transformation by virtue of the Buddha’s great vows and profound merit.
17. The Division of the Size of the Jewel Ponds. Chapter Seventeen. The Buddha said:

“The lecture halls and palaces within the realm of Amitābha Buddha surpass those inhabited by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, in the sixth heaven of this world by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions; they can never be equaled.”
Within and without, there are further natural flowing springs and various ponds that arise spontaneously together with the seven precious jewels.
There are some ponds composed of a single type of jewel, where even the sand on the bottom consists of that same single jewel;
if it is a pond of gold, the bottom has silver sand; if it is a crystal pond, the bottom has lapis lazuli sand; and if it is a coral pond, the bottom has amber sand.
Regarding those ponds composed of two jewels, their bottom sands are likewise made of those two jewels;
if the pond is of gold or silver, its bottom sand is of crystal and lapis lazuli;
if the pond is of crystal or lapis lazuli, its bottom sand is of coral and amber.
If it is a pond of coral or amber, the sand at its bottom consists of *śukti* (mother-of-pearl) and *musāragalva* (agate).
If it is a pond composed of three, four, or even seven precious substances together, the sand at its bottom is likewise composed of those same substances.

Among these various jeweled ponds, there are those that are forty li square, those that are fifty li square, and those that are sixty li square; thus they increase in size progressively until they reach twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li, like a great ocean.
However, these various ponds are all places where Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and other superior virtuous beings grow and dwell, and they occasionally bathe therein.

If those Buddha-ponds were to exist, their dimensions would be twice as large; they are formed by the intermingling of the seven treasures, with white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi-jewels serving as the sand upon their bottoms.
These ponds are all filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues; it is pure, fragrant, and clean, with a flavor like nectar.

Within them there are furthermore a hundred kinds of extraordinary flowers, each with a thousand petals; their colors and radiance are diverse, and their fragrances are likewise distinct, so rich and pervasive as to be beyond description.
**Chapter 18: On Rebirth by Transformation within Lotus Flowers** The Buddha said:

"In the countless worlds of the ten directions, all the devas and humans, down to the smallest crawling insects and wriggling creatures, who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, are all born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds made of the seven precious substances. They grow naturally without anyone to nurse them, and they all partake of natural food."
Their countenances and physical forms are upright, pure, and beautiful; they are certainly beyond comparison with those of the mundane world, nor can they be compared even to devas or humans;
all have received naturally pure and empty bodies and infinite lifespans.
19. Chapter Nineteen: On Categorization by Analogy. The Buddha said:
"Suppose there were a commoner standing beside an emperor; could their deportment possibly be compared?"
Ānanda replied: "The *ṛṣabha* stands by the side of the sovereign;
its emaciated, wretched, and hideous appearance is beyond comparison, such that even a hundred thousand million times [the beauty of others] cannot approach it."

The reason for this is that they all failed to plant the roots of virtue in their previous lives; they accumulated wealth but did not practice giving, becoming increasingly stingy as they grew rich, desiring only empty gains and greedily seeking more without ever being satisfied.
Lacking faith, they do not cultivate goodness to obtain blessings, but instead commit various evils; thus, when their lives end, they fall into the evil realms and undergo long-lasting suffering.
Even if they emerge to become human beings, they are lowly, base, and ugly, such that all who see them can witness it.

That emperors and kings are honored and noble among men is entirely due to the accumulation of merit in previous lives. Being compassionate, kind, gentle, and virtuous; practicing extensive charity and universal salvation; sacrificing themselves for the benefit of others; and remaining free from conflict or contention—thereby, at the end of their lives, they ought to be reborn in the heavens to enjoy their blessings and pleasures.
That residual fortune still persists leads them to be born into royal families, naturally noble and distinguished, with upright and handsome features, revered and served by all.
Fine garments and precious delicacies are provided according to their wishes; were it not for the merit of past lives, how could this be so?
The Buddha said, "What you say is correct! As for physical form and majestic radiance,

although a sovereign is the most honored among men, compared to a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), he is like something vulgar and base— as if that commoner were standing by the side of the sovereign."
The Wheel-Turning Sage King is the foremost in the world; compared to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he cannot approach even a hundred-thousand-millionth part.
Compared to the King of the Sixth Heaven, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven likewise cannot approach even a hundred-thousand-millionth part.

The sixth heavenly king, when compared to the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and all the most virtuous persons within the land of Amitābha Buddha, falls short by a factor of hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions; he cannot possibly equal them.
20. Section on Cleansing the Body. The twentieth section, "Cleansing the Body," states:

The Buddha said, "In the land of Amitābha Buddha, when the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and all those excellent beings enter the ponds made of the seven treasures to cleanse their bodies, if they wish for the water to reach their feet, the water immediately reaches their feet;
if they wish for it to reach their knees, the water immediately reaches their knees; if they wish for it to reach their waists or armpits, up to their necks, the water does likewise."
If he wishes to pour it over his body so that it is entirely according to his will, and if he wishes for the water to become as it was before, it immediately becomes so.

Its temperature, whether warm or cold, is perfectly harmonized and agreeable; it awakens the spirit, gladdens the body, and cleanses all anxieties and deliberations. It is clear, pure, and limpid, as if it were formless.
Having finished bathing, each sat upon a lotus flower; naturally, a gentle breeze stirred, blowing through the various jewel trees, producing either music or Dharma sounds.
It blew upon the various jewel flowers, which all became extraordinary fragrances, scattering over the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and the great multitude.

The flowers that fell to the ground accumulated to a thickness of four inches; they were brilliant and beautiful as far as the eye could see, with an incomparable fragrance. When they began to slightly wither, a natural wind blew them away.

Among the assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the great multitude, there were those who wished to hear the sound of the Dharma, those who wished to hear music, those who wished to hear the fragrance of flowers, and those who wished to hear nothing at all;

those who wished to hear would each hear it alone, while those who did not wish to hear remained silent and heard nothing. Each was satisfied according to their own inclination without any discord, and they experienced a constant, spontaneous joy.
21. Section on Advancing in Practice after Finishing the Bath. Section Twenty-one. The Buddha said:

"When everyone has finished bathing, each shall go forth to cultivate and advance their practice. Some shall discourse upon the sutras on the ground; some shall recite the sutras on the ground; some shall explain the sutras to themselves on the ground; some shall orally transmit the sutras on the ground; some shall listen to the sutras on the ground; some shall contemplate the sutras on the ground; some shall reflect upon the Way on the ground; some shall sit in meditation with single-minded concentration on the ground; and some shall practice walking meditation on the ground."

There were still those who preached the sutras in mid-air, those who recited the sutras in mid-air, those who expounded the sutras on their own in mid-air, those who orally transmitted the sutras in mid-air, those who listened to the sutras in mid-air, those who chanted the sutras in mid-air, those who contemplated the Way in mid-air, those who sat in single-minded meditation in mid-air, and those who practiced the path in mid-air.
Among them, those who had not yet attained the stage of *srotāpanna* attained the stage of *srotāpanna* because of this;
those who had not yet attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* because of this;
and those who had not yet attained the stage of *anāgāmin* attained the stage of *anāgāmin*.
Those who had not yet attained arhatship attained arhatship;
those who had not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression became bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression.
Each, according to their own capacity, attained what they could; there was none who was not joyful, at ease, and delighted.

Section Twenty-two: Pooling the Flow of the Dharma-Sound. Part Two of Section Twenty-two.
The Buddha said:

Within the various jewel ponds, the waters flow into one another, neither too slowly nor too quickly. The waves give rise to immeasurable, natural, wondrous sounds: some produce the sound of preaching the Buddha; some the sound of preaching the Dharma; some the sound of preaching the Saṃgha; some the sound of preaching tranquility; some the sound of preaching emptiness and non-self; some the sound of preaching great compassion; some the sound of preaching the pāramitās; some the sound of preaching the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities; some the sound of preaching the various supernormal knowledges; some the sound of preaching non-action; some the sound of preaching non-arising and non-ceasing; some the sound of preaching supreme patience; and even the sound of preaching all wondrous dharmas, such as the consecration of ambrosia.

Such sounds as these accord with their respective desires; there is none who hears them who does not experience immeasurable joy, give rise to a pure mind, and become free from all conceptual discrimination. They become upright and impartial, ripening their roots of goodness, and shall never regress from unsurpassed bodhi.

In that world, one no longer hears of the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or yakṣas; nor does one hear any such evil sounds as killing, stealing, strife, harsh speech, or double-tongued speech—such sounds are utterly unheard of, let alone their actual existence!
"There are only sounds that are naturally pure and matters that are naturally joyful; for this reason, that land is named 'Ultimate Bliss.
23. Section on the Flowering Trees on the Banks of the Ponds, Part Two: The Buddha said:
"Upon the banks of the various jewel ponds, there are countless sandalwood trees and auspicious fruit trees, whose flowers and fruits are perpetually fragrant, and whose scents waft everywhere."
Furthermore, there were celestial utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers; variegated in color, radiant and luxuriant, they completely covered the surface of the water.
Furthermore, there were seven kinds of jewel trees. Among them, those consisting of a single type of jewel had their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all made of that one jewel.
Those consisting of two jewels had their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits interspersed with two types of jewels.
Those consisting of three jewels had their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits interspersed with three types of jewels.
Regarding those trees composed of four jewels, the roots, trunks, branches, and leaves each consist of one jewel, while their flowers and fruits are identical to the roots and trunks.
Regarding those trees composed of five jewels, the roots, trunks, branches, leaves, and flowers each consist of one jewel, while the fruits are identical to the roots.
Regarding those trees composed of six jewels, the roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits each consist of one jewel.
The manner in which each tree is composed of the seven treasures is likewise so; it is only that the addition of a single treasure is applied to each successive joint.

Thus, these various trees stand in distinct rows, with row upon row planted together, stem facing stem, branch aligned with branch, leaf directed toward leaf, flower following flower, and fruit corresponding to fruit. Such rows extend for hundreds of thousands of li, interspersed with jeweled ponds.

Furthermore, in this manner, throughout the entire world, its radiant splendor was so magnificent that it could not be fully beheld; gentle breezes arose at intervals, spontaneously producing subtle and exquisite sounds beyond compare.
24. Chapter on the Wondrous Music of Tree Sounds, the Twenty-fourth. The Buddha said:

"The ten thousand kinds of music possessed by a worldly monarch are not equal to even a single note of the music of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), surpassing it by hundreds of thousands of millions of times."
The ten thousand kinds of music of a wheel-turning sage king are not equal to even a single note of the music of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven king, by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions.

The ten thousand kinds of musical instruments of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are not equal to even a single note among the various musical sounds of the King of the Sixth Heaven; they do not compare to it by even a hundred thousand million times.

The ten thousand kinds of musical sounds of the sixth heavenly king are not equal to even a single sound from the various seven-jeweled trees within the land of Amitābha Buddha; they fall short by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions.

Furthermore, there were various kinds of spontaneous and wondrous music, the sounds of which were none other than the sublime Dharma; they were clear, resonant, exquisite, harmonious, and elegant, being the most supreme among all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
25. Section on Spontaneous Food and Drink, Number Twenty-Five. The Buddha said:

"Regarding those who have been reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, when it is time for them to eat and drink, if there are those who desire silver bowls, those who desire gold bowls, those who desire bowls of crystal or lapis lazuli, or those who desire bowls of coral, amber, tridacna shell, or agate; or if they desire bowls made of moon-pearls, maṇi-jewels, white jade, purple gold, or the like—all such vessels appear before them, manifested according to their wishes."
Within it, food and drink of a hundred flavors abound; whether sour, salty, pungent, or bland, each is exactly as desired—neither excessive nor deficient.
Nor does one eat excessively for the sake of delicacy, but only to sustain and benefit one's physical strength;
once eaten, it naturally dissolves without leaving any residue.
Or, one may simply perceive the color or smell and take that as food.

They vanish spontaneously; when they wish to eat again, they reappear as before. That world-system is supremely pure, secure, subtle, and blissful, following which lies the path of unconditioned Nirvana.
26. Section on the Excellence of the Environment. Section Twenty-Six on the Excellence of the Environment. The Buddha said:
"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, there are only bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and various superior virtuous persons; there are no women."

All have lifespans of incalculable kalpas; all possess the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience, seeing one another from afar and hearing each other’s voices from a distance; they are all seekers of the Path of Goodness, with none being otherwise.

Their countenances were all upright, pure, and handsome, free from any ugliness; their natures were all characterized by wisdom and vigor, free from any mediocrity or folly. Whatever they wished to say was already known in advance;

whatever their minds and hearts contemplated was nothing other than the Way and its Virtue (*moralò*); whatever manifested in their speech was nothing other than righteous matters. They all loved and respected one another, with no instances of hatred or envy; they all acted in harmony and order, without any discord. may I accumulate manifold virtues so that my own buddha-field shall likewise be so.

**33. Bodhisattvas Bringing Offerings, Part Three** The Buddha said:

According to their every wish, countless articles of offering—such as fragrant flowers, music, garments, canopies, banners, and streamers—spontaneously manifested before them.

Chapter 34: The Section on the Merits of Bodhisattvas The Buddha said: "In the land of Amitābha Buddha, the assembly of bodhisattvas have gentle and harmonious countenances and are fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence.

They have attained unimpeded mastery in meditative concentration and wisdom; their supernatural powers and majestic virtues are all perfected. They have entered deeply into the Dharma-gates and attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), having reached the ultimate clarity of all bodhisattva paths."
Having subdued the sense faculties, their bodies and minds were supple; they dwelt in tranquility and attained parinirvāṇa, entering deeply into right wisdom without further residual habits.

Relying on the seven factors of enlightenment—the noble path practiced by the Buddhas—they cultivated the five eyes to illuminate the ultimate truth and penetrate conventional reality, possessing unimpeded mastery in eloquence and dhāraṇī.

He is skillfully adept in the boundless expedient means of the world; his words are truthful and he penetrates deeply into the flavor of their meaning. He expounds the True Dharma to extensively deliver sentient beings, removing all the afflictions and sufferings of those beings.

He contemplates the three realms as empty and non-existent, knowing that all phenomena are entirely quiescent—without marks, unconditioned, without cause, without fruit, without grasping, without relinquishing, without bondage, and without liberation. Having eliminated all conceptual discrimination and distanced himself from perversions, he is firm and immovable like Mount Sumeru.

Wisdom is as clear and bright as the sun and moon; it is as vast as the ocean, producing the jewels of merit; it blazes like fire, consuming the fuel of afflictions; it is as patient as the earth, equal toward all things; and it is as pure as water, washing away all dust and defilements.
Like space, which is boundless and does not obstruct anything; like a lotus flower emerging from the water, free from all defilement;
like the sound of thunder, which resounds with the voice of the Dharma; like gathering clouds, which bring down the rain of the Dharma;
like the wind moving trees, which causes the sprouts of Bodhi to grow; and like the cry of a bull-king, which is distinct from that of other cattle.
Like a dragon-elephant, his majestic power is difficult to fathom; like a fine horse, his gait and carriage are without fail;
like a lion throne, he is free from fear; like a nyagrodha tree, he provides shade for the great assembly;
like an udumbara flower, he is difficult to encounter; like a vajra-pestle, he shatters the mountains of heterodoxy; and like the Brahma King.
Because his body is born among the Brahma-multitude; because he is like the garuḍa, who surpasses the venomous dragon; because he is like a bird in the sky, leaving no trace of its dwelling;
because he is like the Snowy Mountains, whose reflected merit is pure; and because he is like Maitreya, who contemplates the dharma-realm as equal.
Dedicated to seeking the Dharma with a mind never weary or satisfied, they constantly desire to expound it widely with a will free from fatigue.

They beat the drum of the Dharma and raise the banner of the Dharma; they cause the sun of wisdom to shine, dispelling the darkness of delusion. Cultivating the six points of harmonious respect, they always act as teachers and guides, serving as lamps for the world and the most supreme field of merit.

He extracts the thorns of all desires to bring peace to all sentient beings; his merit is so preeminent that there are none who do not revere him. He has respectfully made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and is constantly praised by all Buddhas together, having brought the various *pāramitās* of a Bodhisattva to ultimate completion.

They cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as all the gateways of samādhi regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, thereby remaining far removed from the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Ānanda! Those bodhisattvas have accomplished such immeasurable merit. I have merely spoken of it for you by way of its essentials;
were I to explain it in detail, even if one were to pass through an entire eon, one could not reach its end.

35. The Section on Those Who Have Attained Parinirvāṇa, the Thirty-fifth. At that time, in the assembly, there was the Bodhisattva Ajita, who rose from his seat, joined his palms, and asked the Buddha:
"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, are there any śrāvakas who have attained parinirvāṇa?"
The Buddha asked,
"Do you see the stars in these four continents? He replied:
“I have already seen them all.
The Buddha said, “Suppose Mahāmaudgalyāyana were to fly through the four continents; in a single day and night, he could know the total number of their stars.”
The assembly of śrāvakas in that land exceeds by hundreds of thousands of billions the number of stars in the four continents; their total number cannot be fully known.
When one of those śrāvakas enters parinirvāṇa, it is like removing a single drop from the great ocean—one does not perceive its depletion.
Although those who have entered parinirvāṇa are numerous, it is like removing the water of a single stream from the great ocean; one does not perceive that it has become less.

Even though those who have entered parinirvāṇa are incalculable, the number of those currently present and those newly attained as śrāvakas is likewise immeasurable and infinite—just as the great ocean, even with the water of a single Gaṅgā River removed, does not appear diminished.
Even if all the waters of the world were made to flow into the sea, it could not be perceived that the volume of the seawater had increased. Why is this?
Because the sea is the sovereign of all the waters of the world, and its capacity for reception is infinite.

It is likewise in that Buddha-field: even though the gods and people from the countless Buddha-fields of the ten directions, down to the smallest crawling and wriggling insects, all go to be reborn therein, they are unable to perceive an increase in the number of people in that field.

Why is this so? Because that land alone stands preeminent among the countless Buddha-fields of the ten directions, being exceedingly vast, exceedingly great, and as expansive as if it were boundless. Why is this so?
"It is because when he was a bodhisattva, his vows were vast, his diligence was tireless, and he accumulated merit without end that he is able to be thus.
36. Section on the Greatness and Smallness of the Radiance, Part Three: Thirty-sixth. The Buddha said:
"Amitābha Buddha and the various bodhisattvas and śrāvakas within his land each have radiance upon their crowns, which differs in its magnitude."
The light from the crowns of the heads of all the śrāvakas each illuminates seven zhang; the light from the crowns of the heads of all the bodhisattvas each illuminates ten billion li.

There are two bodhisattvas who are foremost among them: one is named Avalokiteśvara and the other is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta; they constantly sit by the Buddha’s side, attending to him and engaging in noble discourse.

The Buddha consulted with the two bodhisattvas regarding the future and present affairs of the worlds in the ten directions; he wished for the two bodhisattvas to go to the abodes of other Buddhas, traveling by means of their supernormal powers as swiftly as the Buddha himself.
He emanates transformation bodies into this world to assist the Buddha in spreading his teachings, yet within those lands he does not lose his presence in the present.

His wisdom and majestic spiritual power are foremost; the light from the crown of his head each illuminates a thousand Buddha-worlds. If there are people of the world—sons or daughters of good family—who encounter urgent distress, terror, or legal troubles, and single-mindedly take refuge in Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, there are none who do not attain liberation.

The radiance from the crown of that Buddha’s head was exceedingly vast and brilliant; because the Buddha’s light was so superior, the sun, moon, and stars in that world were rendered without luster, and they all remained suspended in the air without revolving.
Consequently, there were no such things as one day or two days, one month or two months, nor were there any reckoning of years or kalpas.

Calculating by these standards, the radiance of that Buddha will persist for incalculable eons after incalculable eons, and again for incalculable eons after incalculable eons—beyond all further reckoning of eons—and there shall never be a time of darkness;
that world’s lack of destruction is likewise the same.
37. The Section on Infinite Gratitude. Part Thirty-Seven. The Buddha said:

“Amitābha Buddha, while teaching and transforming the world, intends to deliver all devas and humans within the countless buddha-fields of the ten directions, even down to the smallest crawling and creeping insects, so that they may all be reborn in his land and cause them all to attain the Way of Nirvāṇa.”
Among them, those who wished to become Buddhas were immediately led to cultivate the bodhisattva practices until they attained Buddhahood.

Once they had become Buddhas, they in turn transformed and taught one another, delivering and liberating the devas and humans throughout the countless worlds of the ten directions, down to the smallest crawling and flying insects;
those reborn in their lands were beyond counting, as were those who became bodhisattvas and subsequently attained Buddhahood.
This merit and virtue of this Buddha extends throughout the worlds of the ten directions, being inexhaustible, limitless, and inconceivable.
Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Lifespan of the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“Do you wish to know whether the lifespan of Amitābha Buddha is infinite?”
Ajita replied, "I truly wish to hear and know it.
The Buddha said:
"Listen clearly!

Suppose all the gods and humans in the countless worlds of the ten directions, down to the smallest crawling insects, were all to become human beings; and suppose they were all to become pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, sitting together in meditation with a single mind, and combining their wisdom into one wisdom. Even if one were to calculate for thousands of billions of kalpas the lifespan of that Buddha, no one would be able to know it."

Who could believe and know this?

39. Section on Successive Attainment of Buddhahood, Part Three. Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:

40. The Section on the Immeasurability of Buddha-Wisdom, Part Forty. Ānanda rose again from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In other world-systems there are all Mount Sumerus; why is it that in the land of Amitābha Buddha alone is this mountain absent?"

The Buddha’s wisdom is also like this.
Suppose one wished to measure and exhaust all the waters of the great oceans with a single person’s peck; your wisdom is likewise so limited.
Throughout the billions upon billions of kalpas of the past, there have been billions upon billions of Buddhas, each with their own distinct name and title, none of whom shared my name, Śākyamuni.

as such kalpas accumulated without end, those whose names and titles were the same as mine were as numerous as the grains of sand flowing along the banks of the Ganges River—one Buddha for every grain of sand. These belonged to the past, and I have seen them all.

Now, as I sit facing south in formal posture, I behold billions upon billions of worlds in the southern direction; within them there are Buddhas, each with their own distinct name and title, none of whom share my name, Śākyamuni.

Furthermore, beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of worlds, there are those whose names are identical to mine; as one passes through such worlds without end, those who bear my name are as numerous as the grains of sand flowing along the banks of the Ganges River—one Buddha for every single grain of sand.
It is likewise in the east, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below; I see all of these belonging to the present.

Throughout billions upon billions of kalpas in the future, there will be billions upon billions of Buddhas, each with their own distinct name and title, none of whom shall have a name and title identical to mine, Śākyamuni.

Furthermore, throughout the interval of billions upon billions of kalpas, there will be those whose name and title are the same as mine; such kalpas shall accumulate without end. Those whose name and title are the same as mine will be as numerous as the grains of sand flowing along the banks of the Ganges River—one Buddha for every grain of sand—and I shall see them all in the future.

Thus one knows that the Buddha’s wisdom can penetrate the worlds of the ten directions—past, future, and present—endless and infinite, inconceivable; how could it be fathomed by the petty intelligence of a mere peck?

“In other worlds, from the third Yāma Heaven up to the seventh Brahmā Heaven, upon what do they rely to dwell? They replied:
"It exists naturally within space.

"In that land there is no Mount Sumeru; the Four Heavenly Kings and the two heavens of the Trāyastriṃśa are likewise absent."
The karmic retributions of the deeds performed by devas and humans are inconceivable;
that these sentient beings abide upon the ground of karma is likewise inconceivable.

Consequently, regarding the sequence of the Buddhas' appearances and the duration of their initial resolve, there have been many errors!
Therefore, I suggest that for each of the Buddhas prior to Amitāyus (Guangyuan Fo), the character "prior" (qian) be added; thus, adding a total of fifty-two instances of the word "prior.

In this way, the chronological order of the fifty-three Awakened Sovereigns appearing in the world, the precise account of the causal ground of the Tathāgata Amitāyus, and the systematic arrangement of time periods will become clear and orderly without confusion; the details of these events will be entirely free from error.
